keyVerseText: Philip, and Bartholomew; Thomas, and Matthew the publican; James the son of Alphaeus, and Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus;
rootMeaning: The name Βαρθολομαῖος (Bartholomaîos) originates from Aramaic, combining בַּר (bar), meaning 'son of,' with תָּלְמַי (Tolmai), a personal name. Thus, it literally means 'son of Tolmai.' This patronymic construction highlights the cultural and linguistic background of the early Christian apostles, grounding Bartholomew's identity in his familial lineage, which adds depth beyond the simple English transliteration 'Bartholomew.'
usageInScripture: The word Βαρθολομαῖος appears four times in the New Testament, consistently translated as 'Bartholomew.' This uniformity in translation reflects the proper noun usage as a personal name, specifically identifying one of the twelve apostles. The consistency across Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Acts underscores Bartholomew's recognized role within the apostolic community without variation or metaphorical extension.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Bartholomew's name as 'son of Tolmai' connects us to the historical and cultural reality of Jesus' followers, emphasizing their rootedness in Jewish and Aramaic heritage. This reminds believers that the apostles were real individuals with tangible backgrounds, chosen by Christ to carry forward the gospel. Recognizing Bartholomew's identity as an apostle affirms the divine calling upon ordinary men, highlighting God's grace in using them as foundational witnesses to Christ's ministry. It also encourages faith in God's sovereign choice and the continuity of His redemptive plan through human history.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 10:3, Bartholomew is listed among the twelve apostles alongside Philip, Thomas, Matthew, James, and Lebbaeus. His inclusion here as 'Bartholomew' affirms his apostolic authority and the personal nature of Jesus' call to discipleship. The use of his name, rooted in 'son of Tolmai,' subtly reminds readers that the gospel was entrusted to individuals with distinct identities and backgrounds, called to participate in the mission of Christ.
